candidates.hidden_signal_to_verify: Whether airline customers are increasing outsourcing to AAR because internal maintenance capacity, engine-shop slots, or parts availability remain constrained.
candidates.next_evidence: Read latest 10-K/10-Q segment disclosures for Parts Supply and Repair & Engineering growth, backlog or committed customer expansion, MRO facility utilization, margin mix, and customer concentration.
candidates.node_relation: Direct aviation-capacity enabler: supplies aircraft parts, repair and engineering services, component support, and airline maintenance-adjacent services that can influence aircraft availability and maintenance turnaround.
candidates.sector_or_industry: Aviation aftermarket services, parts distribution, repair and engineering, integrated aviation solutions
candidates.theme_relation: If consumer travel demand keeps aircraft utilization high, airlines may need more outsourced parts supply, used-serviceable-material, warranty management, and MRO support to keep fleets in service.
candidates.why_include: AAR is a public, mid-cap aviation services company with explicit exposure to parts supply, repair and engineering, integrated solutions, and commercial aviation demand. Its role is closer to the aircraft-availability chokepoint than to headline consumer travel brands.
candidates.why_underfollowed: It is usually screened as aerospace/industrial services rather than consumer travel, despite being tied to airline fleet utilization and maintenance capacity.

candidates.hidden_signal_to_verify: Whether growth is driven by structural aircraft-parts scarcity and exclusive OEM distribution wins rather than only acquisitions or cyclical restocking.
candidates.next_evidence: Check organic growth, acquisition integration, leverage after large deals, OEM-exclusive distribution agreements, MRO capacity additions, and whether commercial aviation customers are broadening.
candidates.node_relation: Direct aviation aftermarket node: distributes parts and provides maintenance, repair, and overhaul services for aircraft components and engine accessories.
candidates.sector_or_industry: Aviation aftermarket distribution and MRO services
candidates.theme_relation: A second-order travel beneficiary if high airline utilization and older fleets increase demand for aftermarket parts, component repair, and engine-accessory MRO.
candidates.why_include: VSE has repositioned toward a pure-play aviation aftermarket platform, making it a cleaner small/mid-cap way to track aviation aftermarket capacity than diversified aerospace primes.
candidates.why_underfollowed: It is not a travel stock in standard consumer screens and may be classified under industrial distribution or aerospace services, even though its revenues can respond to airline maintenance and parts scarcity.

candidates.hidden_signal_to_verify: Whether subscription growth is coming from property-level operational bottlenecks such as labor efficiency, mobile ordering, payments, PMS modernization, and resort/casino complexity.
candidates.next_evidence: Review customer wins, subscription net retention, implementation backlog, mix of hotels/resorts/cruise/casino customers, and whether sales cycles accelerate during periods of travel-volume strength.
candidates.node_relation: Lodging and venue operating-system enabler: provides hospitality-focused property management, point-of-sale, payments, inventory/procurement, and related software.
candidates.theme_relation: If hotels, resorts, casinos, cruise ships, stadiums, and managed foodservice operators face staffing shortages and guest-volume complexity, mission-critical operations software can become a capacity and efficiency lever.
candidates.why_include: Agilysys is a public, mid-cap software company focused specifically on hospitality operations rather than general enterprise software. Its exposure is to the operational layer that can help hotels and travel venues handle more guests with constrained labor.
candidates.why_underfollowed: It is usually categorized as software/SaaS, not as a travel-capacity beneficiary, and its customer impact is embedded inside hotel and venue operations.

candidates.company: Grupo Aeroportuario del Centro Norte, S.A.B. de C.V.
candidates.hidden_signal_to_verify: Whether passenger growth translates into pricing, concession revenue, and capex-approved capacity expansion, or whether regulation and concession terms cap upside.
candidates.next_evidence: Track monthly passenger reports, master development program capex, tariff regulation, non-aeronautical revenue per passenger, concession changes, and airline route concentration.
candidates.node_relation: Regulated airport-capacity asset: operates Mexican airports and reports passenger traffic, making it a direct node for terminal throughput, passenger-processing capacity, commercial airport services, and regional travel infrastructure.
candidates.sector_or_industry: Airport operator and regulated airport infrastructure
candidates.theme_relation: US-listed ADR gives public-market exposure to travel infrastructure rather than airlines or online booking platforms. Passenger growth can pressure terminals, capex plans, commercial concessions, parking, and aeronautical-service economics.
candidates.why_include: OMAB is a US-listed airport operator with direct passenger-throughput exposure. It fits the node as a capacity owner rather than a consumer-facing travel brand.
candidates.why_underfollowed: It is an ADR for Mexican airport infrastructure and is often missed by US consumer-discretionary screens, despite being tied to air-travel volume and airport capacity economics.

memory_update.text: AIR is a priority underfollowed candidate for the travel-capacity node because aircraft availability and MRO/parts constraints may matter more than airline demand alone.

VSEC is a priority underfollowed candidate for aviation aftermarket exposure; key survival tests are organic growth, leverage, and whether OEM distribution/MRO wins are structurally tied to fleet-utilization bottlenecks.
AGYS maps to the hospitality staffing/software bottleneck rather than headline travel demand; verify recurring revenue quality, customer wins, and labor-efficiency value proposition.
OMAB adds a regulated airport-infrastructure lane; useful for tracking passenger-throughput capacity, concession economics, and capex/tariff constraints.

US-listed pure-play baggage-handling and ground-handling vendors remain hard to identify because many major operators are private, foreign-listed, subsidiaries, or embedded inside diversified industrials; later layers should search ADRs/OTC and parent-company segment disclosures.

node: Travel capacity enablers: airport services, baggage handling, maintenance, lodging operations software, and local experience infrastructure
summary: Expanded the underfollowed discovery lane for travel-capacity enablers. The strongest US-listed candidates found in this pass sit one or two layers away from obvious travel demand: aviation aftermarket parts and MRO capacity, hospitality operating software, and airport concession/regulated infrastructure. The lane is intentionally not airlines, hotels, cruise lines, or online travel agencies; those remain demand indicators and customer/context anchors. No investment recommendation is made.
